title: ISC2 CISSP-ISSAP
summary: The Information Systems Security Architecture Professional (ISSAP) is a concentration exam from ISC2 for holders of the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) who specialise in security architecture. It sits at an advanced level and suits senior architects, security engineers and consultants who design controls for large or complex organisations. It proves to an employer that you can turn business needs into an architecture, choose cryptographic and identity solutions, and defend design choices to executives and auditors. The exam covers six published domains, including identity and access management, security architecture models, and the security operations and governance that support them; it uses multiple choice items written at a much deeper level than the core CISSP exam. It leads to roles such as security architect, enterprise architect, principal consultant and technical security lead. This is an independent study guide that is not official ISC2 material; confirm the current exam outline with the vendor before booking.

beginner.definition: The Information Systems Security Architecture Professional (ISSAP) is an advanced certification from ISC2. It is only open to people who already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP). It focuses on designing security for large systems, rather than on running them day by day.
beginner.whyItMatters: Architects decide how a whole system will be protected before it is built. Those choices are hard and costly to change later. This certificate proves you can make them well. It is a strong signal for senior roles and for consultancy work. It also deepens the knowledge you already proved in the core CISSP exam.
howItWorks: Check that you hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) and meet the rules for taking a concentration exam.
Read the official ISC2 exam outline and list the domains with the tasks under each one.
Study security architecture models and the frameworks that large organisations use.
Go deeper on cryptography, identity and access management, and network design.
Practise scenario questions that ask which design best meets a stated business need.
The exam is multiple choice and is separate from the core exam, so plan several months of study.
beginner.example: Imagine a company that wants one login for staff, partners and customers. A junior engineer may reach for a single large directory. An architect asks harder questions. How do we prove who a partner is, what happens when their system is offline, and how do we remove access the same day a contract ends? The architecture answer often combines several services with clear trust rules. The ISSAP exam tests that kind of thinking.
takeaways: You must already hold the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) before you sit this exam.
The questions are deeper, so study design trade offs and not only definitions.
Learn to justify a design to a business audience as well as to engineers.

objectives: Translate business and regulatory needs into security architecture requirements
Compare architecture models and choose one that fits the organisation
Choose cryptographic controls and explain the trade offs to decision makers
Design identity and access management for staff, partners and customers
Plan security monitoring, response and recovery as part of the architecture
Assess how a design change affects risk, cost and compliance

chapters.title: Architect for governance, compliance, risk and security strategy
objectives: Gather business, legal and regulatory needs and turn them into architecture requirements
Choose architecture models and frameworks that suit the organisation
Set out security strategy and roadmaps that senior leaders can approve
Show how a design meets compliance duties in other countries
Define architecture principles and standards that project teams must follow

chapters.title: Architect for security operations
objectives: Design logging, monitoring and detection across a large estate
Plan incident response, forensics and recovery as architecture components
Set service levels that keep security operations effective
Design change and configuration control for critical systems
Plan how the architecture will be tested and assured

chapters.title: Architect for identity and access management
objectives: Design identity lifecycle processes for staff, partners and customers
Choose authentication methods and levels of assurance for each population
Design authorisation models such as role based or attribute based access
Plan federation and single sign on across separate organisations
Design privileged access controls and regular access review

chapters.title: Architect for security engineering and cryptography
objectives: Select cryptographic algorithms and key lengths that fit the data and the risk
Design key management, including generation, storage, rotation and recovery
Choose controls for data at rest, data in motion and data in use
Plan for emerging threats such as attacks on widely used algorithms
Review cryptographic design choices with independent experts

chapters.title: Architect for physical and logical infrastructure security
objectives: Design network zoning and segmentation that limit the spread of an attack
Choose controls for wireless, remote access and cloud connectivity
Plan physical protection for sites, equipment and utilities
Design resilience, redundancy and backup for critical services
Assess the security of third party and hosted infrastructure

chapters.title: Architect for secure delivery of services
objectives: Build security into development and delivery methods such as agile
Define security requirements and acceptance criteria for suppliers
Design secure deployment, patching and release processes
Plan how services will be decommissioned and data safely removed
Measure whether the delivered architecture still meets its original goals
